theme: The Entry; controversies; the widow’s offering; signs of the end
readingInstruction: Read Luke 19:28-21:38. The King rides into Jerusalem, weeps over the city, cleanses the temple, and teaches there while the leaders try to trap him. It ends with his words about the end of the age. Read it as the week before the cross.
settingTheScene: The long journey is over. Jesus comes to Jerusalem at the time of Passover. For the next few days he teaches in the temple, answering questions from priests, scribes, Pharisees, Sadducees, and the Herodians. Each group tries to catch him in his words, and each is silenced. Luke records the events in an orderly way, and the shadow of the cross lies over every scene.
observation: “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” (19:38).
“Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace!” (19:42).
“It is written, And my house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers” (19:46).
“The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (20:17).
“Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (20:25).
“Now he is not God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him” (20:38).
“Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them” (21:3).
“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (21:33).
interpretation:
Jesus sends two disciples for a colt that no one has ever ridden. As he rides toward the city, the crowd of disciples spreads cloaks on the road and cries out, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” Zechariah 9:9 is being fulfilled. When the Pharisees ask him to rebuke them, he says that if they were silent, the very stones would cry out.

But as he draws near and sees the city, he weeps. He knows that Jerusalem does not recognize the time of her visitation, and he foretells its destruction, which came in AD 70. The King who enters in triumph weeps for those who reject him.

In the temple he drives out those who sell, saying the house is meant to be a house of prayer. Then he teaches daily, and the chief priests and scribes seek to destroy him but cannot find a way, because all the people hang on his words.

They challenge his authority, and he answers with a question about John’s baptism. They will not answer, so neither will he. Then he tells the parable of the wicked tenants. A man plants a vineyard and sends servants, who are beaten, and finally his beloved son, whom they kill. This is the story of Israel’s leaders and of Jesus himself. He quotes Psalm 118: the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone.

Then come the traps. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar? “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, ask about the woman married to seven brothers. Jesus answers that those who rise are like angels and that God is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, “not God of the dead but of the living.” Then Jesus asks his own question: how can the Christ be David’s son, when David calls him Lord (Psalm 110)? Because he is both. Jesus warns against the scribes who devour widows’ houses, and then points out a poor widow who put in two small coins. She gave all she had.

The last chapter is the Olivet discourse, speaking of the destruction of the temple, persecution, signs in the sun, moon, and stars, and the coming of the Son of Man with power and great glory. Jesus’ call is: “Straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” Stay awake, and pray that you may have strength to stand before the Son of Man. Interpreters differ on how to divide what refers to AD 70 and what refers to the end of the age, but the pastoral aim is clear: be watchful, and do not be afraid.
connection: Zechariah 9:9 is the prophecy of the humble king on a donkey. Psalm 118:22-26 is the background to the crowd’s shout and the cornerstone. Isaiah 5:1-7 is the vineyard song behind the tenants. Psalm 110:1 is the verse Jesus asks about. Jeremiah 7:11 is the “den of robbers.” Daniel 7:13-14 describes the Son of Man coming with the clouds. Exodus 3:6 is the verse Jesus cites for the resurrection. Romans 13:1-7 teaches about the state.
application:
Welcome Jesus as King today. Is there an area of your life where you would rather he not enter?

Give something to God out of what you need, not just out of your surplus, like the widow.

Practice watchfulness. Pray for strength for whatever is ahead.
prayerPrompts: Welcome Jesus as King, and tell him what you want to lay at his feet.
Ask him to give you tears for what he weeps over.
Ask him to teach you to give, like the widow, all you have.
